title: Bound, Unbound and Escape
subtitle: Find out what decides whether something comes back
body:
Step 1 of 24 read

How hard would you have to throw it?

Throw a ball and it comes down. Throw it harder and it comes down further away. Newton asked the obvious next question, in a thought experiment he drew in 1687: put a cannon on a mountain so tall it is above the air, and fire it horizontally. What happens if you keep loading more gunpowder?

His answer was that at some point the ground curves away underneath the cannonball as fast as the ball falls, and it stops coming down at all. It goes all the way round and hits you in the back. That is an orbit, and it is the reason a satellite stays up: not because it has escaped gravity, but because it is falling and continually missing.

And if you load even more gunpowder? At some speed it leaves and does not come back. Somewhere between those two outcomes there is a dividing line. Finding that line, and understanding what decides which side of it something falls on, is the whole of this investigation.

Over the next few steps you will fire Newton's cannon yourself.

💡 Nothing needs measuring yet. The panel on the right will appear in a moment with a cannon on it.

title: Bound, Unbound and Escape
subtitle: Find out what decides whether something comes back
body:
Step 24 of 24 read

What you worked out

You started by firing a cannon and asking a question a child could ask: does it come back? By the end you were able to answer the same question about an object from another star system, using one number.

The five things worth keeping:

Gravity never switches off. An escaping object is still being pulled backwards the whole way out. It escapes anyway.

Bound means trapped. Total energy below zero: the object cannot reach infinity, so gravity always turns it round eventually.

Unbound means gone. Total energy above zero: it leaves and is still moving when it is far away.

Escape speed is the dividing line, the speed at which the total comes out exactly zero.

It depends on where you are, not just what you are leaving. More mass raises it. Starting further out lowers it.

That last point is why there is no single answer to "how fast do you have to go to escape the Earth". It depends where you start. And it is why the honest way to ask the question was never about speed at all. It was about energy.

💡 The same test decides much bigger questions: whether a star escapes the cluster it was born in, whether a galaxy holds on to the gas blown out by its supernovae, and whether the Milky Way and Andromeda are bound to each other. They are.
